name: Daria Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the violin desks in a local orchestra, record practice tracks for its young players and teach three private pupils. A master’s in music taught me the scores; years of rehearsal taught me when a young bow hand needs patience.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What presses on that work at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner drives a bus on shifts, and we trade school pickup for our two children. The orchestra pays less than a lead chair should, and our mortgage leaves just three weeks of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the younger players that tidy emails are welcome but a machine cannot bow alongside them. I would ask the orchestra for real paid rehearsal dates rather than a hopeful season outline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our reserve is three weeks and the bus rota changes, so a cancelled concert is already a household problem. There are few other senior violin seats nearby even if AI stays mostly quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would keep leading rehearsals, recording paid practice tracks and teaching my three pupils. I use AI now and then to draft a programme note, but I check names and dates against the printed programme before anyone sees it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about ordinary cancellations and the mortgage. A plateau would not erase my worry about cancelled orchestra pay and our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a concert last disappear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The spring hall repair cancelled two performances. I would ask for a written cancellation fee before next season so my partner can plan bus shifts around actual pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you lean on relatives for pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister can sometimes help, but I would ask her first rather than assume free childcare. A paid date must still be worth her evening.

I would ask for a **written cancellation fee** before next season.
think: Our **three-week reserve** makes cancelled concerts serious while the mortgage and school bills still arrive.
Few **nearby senior seats** offer a quick replacement.
do: Keep **paid rehearsals**, practice tracks and three pupils this week.
Request **written rehearsal dates** and a cancellation fee before next season.
feel: I feel **anxious** about existing concert gaps and mortgage payments.
S0.quote: A plateau would not erase my worry about cancelled orchestra pay and our mortgage.
fieldNote: Her **thin cushion** and shifting bus rota make cancelled calls matter even in a plateau.
Existing **occasional AI notes** receive manual name and date checks.

steps.text: Keep paid orchestra rehearsals, practice recordings and three violin pupils
Request written paid dates and cancellation fee before next season

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the board that generated practice tracks might help children at home, but someone must still teach them to listen. I would ask which recording and coaching hours remain paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Practice tracks are a quarter of my own fees, and cheap tools could remove those commissions. If the orchestra also cuts coaching hours, three weeks of savings will not carry us far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would ask for written paid recording and coaching hours. In the first year I would attend a paid librarian demonstration of a new part checker, then test only my own nameless violin part if the orchestra approves in-house storage; I would play each suggestion against the score and stop if notes change wrongly or the file leaves the library.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel anxious about losing a quarter of my pay. I can learn a proven tool, but I still need paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a child’s part go into the checker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, pupil names stay inside the orchestra school. I would use my own clean part and return to paper if its storage rule fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you apply elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if our paid coaching actually falls. I would seek a posted paid section-leader seat if my master’s qualifies, written net pay after travel replaces lost hours and pickup fits the bus rota; I would stay until a written offer is signed.

say: I would ask for **written recording hours** and paid coaching.
I would tell the board **live coaching** still needs a paid teacher.
think: Practice tracks make up **one-quarter** of my own monthly musician fees.
Lost **coaching hours** would further strain our three-week reserve.
do: Request **written paid hours** for recording and coaching next month.
Test **part checker** after paid training and in-house storage approval on my nameless part; play and stop on errors/leakage.
Apply for a **posted leader seat** after coaching cuts only if qualified, written net after travel replaces losses and pickup fits.
feel: I feel **anxious** about likely recording-fee losses.

fieldNote: The **tool test** needs paid instruction, approved library storage, a nameless owned part and manual playing.

Request written paid recording and coaching hours next month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our board that AGI by 2028 may produce practice tracks before I finish tuning. They owe the players a signed calendar of actual paid rehearsal and coaching hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect recording fees to end in 2028, and some families may drop lessons if software looks cheap. Playing robots come around 2031, three years later. The first lost quarter of my violin income does not wait for playing robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would total track invoices and ask the orchestra for a signed paid calendar. In the first year after 2028, if coaching hours or pupils fall too, I would apply for a posted arts-centre violin lead only if my master’s qualifies, written net pay after travel covers lost fees and the hours fit pickup; I would keep paid orchestra calls and pupils until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel anxious about the expected loss of recording fees and our three-week reserve. If tracks and coaching or pupils went together, I would be alarmed because that is most of my income. I have spent nights calculating whether the savings reach the next mortgage date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for another certificate now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if an actual posted job requires it and a funded place or paid study hours exist. I cannot take tuition from our mortgage money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a rumoured opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A genuine posting and signed net offer come before I leave any paid seat.

I would seek a **posted violin lead** if coaching or pupil work falls.

Keep **paid calls and pupils** until a suitable written offer is signed.
feel: I feel **anxious** about expected recording loss; losing live work too would alarm me.
S2.quote: The first lost quarter of my violin income does not wait for playing robots.
fieldNote: Her **2028 recording loss** precedes physical robot playing around 2031.
The **lead move** needs actual additional losses, a qualified posted opening, written net pay, pickup and offer.

steps.text: Apply for posted violin lead after coaching/pupil loss; written net after travel covers fees, pickup fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the families that five years before AGI by 2031 is time to give young players a paid place to learn together. I would try a chamber workshop only if every adult helping is paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tracks could stop paying by 2031, but a small workshop might replace some recording fees. Playing robots around 2034 add a later risk; I would not promise a new income before parents pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I would price a six-week violin workshop only if the school offers a room after pickup and eight families prepay enough for room hire, inspected loan violins, a paid assistant and my teaching and preparation time. In the first year after 2031 I would renew only if eight places still cover those costs, a room and inspected instruments remain and pickup works; I would keep the private pupils if they do not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until a group covers both wages. Our small reserve cannot pay an assistant in advance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who inspects the borrowed violins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school technician must check strings, bridges and bows before a child uses one. If that cannot happen, the family brings a safe instrument or I cancel that place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if four families prepay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four fees cannot cover the room, assistant or my preparation. I would refund them and continue the three private lessons.

feel: I feel **anxious** because thin savings cannot float assistant pay.
S3.quote: Our small reserve cannot pay an assistant in advance.
fieldNote: The **workshop gate** is eight prepayments for room, inspected instruments and both adults’ time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the younger violinists that ten years before AGI by 2036 gives time for paid apprenticeships, not free work dressed as opportunity. A rehearsal is worth a wage when the chairs are filled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Recording income may end by 2036 and playing robots may reach the pit around 2039. But a low-paid lead chair and three weeks saved already leave us exposed now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this term I would ask the orchestra for a two-year written paid coaching agreement and save five percent of each extra paid wedding-quartet fee after the mortgage, food and instrument repairs, aiming for two months. In the first year after 2036 I would keep paid coaching and apply for a posted conservatory violin tutor role only if my master’s qualifies, written net pay after travel covers lost orchestra fees and pickup fits; I would leave current work only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would remain anxious because even a decade does not pay this month’s mortgage. A written agreement and paid spare fees give me a way to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are wedding fees dependable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I save only when a wedding actually pays after bills; I will not count an unbooked Saturday as money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a prestigious unpaid tutoring role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A title without a written wage cannot support our children or the mortgage.

I would take a **tutor role** only for written pay.
think: **Recording fees** may end by 2036 before 2039 playing robots.
Our **thin reserve** is already a problem this term.
do: Request a **written paid coaching agreement** this term.
Save five percent of **extra paid wedding fees** after mortgage, food and instrument repairs toward two months.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the recording work may vanish before another paid lead seat appears. Signed coaching hours, a posted qualified job and pickup that fits the bus rota would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the assistant at a children’s workshop. Goodwill does not replace a wage for the second adult in the room.

headlineQuote: Goodwill does not replace a wage for the second adult in the room.
portrait: At **43**, Daria leads violin desks with a music master’s, two children, a mortgage and three weeks saved.
Her **lower pay** comes from orchestra coaching, practice recordings and three pupils in a town with few similar jobs.
She tests a **new part checker** only after paid instruction, approved storage and manual playing on her nameless part.
A **paid workshop** needs eight prepayments for room, inspected violins, assistant pay and her teaching and preparation.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase recording work before another paid lead seat opens.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed coaching hours**, a qualified posted job with net pay and child pickup fitting the bus rota would help.
